articles.excerpt: Monitoring ArubaOS exposure after CVE-2026-79850 CVE-2026-79850 shows why a product fingerprint and a vulnerability record answer different questions. HPE Networking ArubaOS 8 has a critical authentic…
articles.body: Monitoring ArubaOS exposure after CVE-2026-79850 CVE-2026-79850 shows why a product fingerprint and a vulnerability record answer different questions. HPE Networking ArubaOS 8 has a critical authentication bypass in specific AOS-8 builds, but an internet search that recognizes ArubaOS cannot determine the installed release, management reachability, or patch history by itself. HPE lists AOS-8.13.0.0 through 8.13.3.0 and AOS-8.10.0.0 through 8.10.0.23 as affected. Fixed versions are 8.13.3.1 and 8.10.0.24. The issue is an unauthenticated remote authentication bypass that can lead to root command execution, scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 and mapped to CWE-288.

articles.title: How We Migrated a Monolith to AWS EC2 and Lived to Tell the Tale
articles.excerpt: What is IaaS, Anyway? Think of moving to the cloud like renting property: SaaS (Software as a Service): Staying in a fully furnished hotel. You just show up and sleep there; you can't repaint the wall…
articles.body: What is IaaS, Anyway? Think of moving to the cloud like renting property: SaaS (Software as a Service): Staying in a fully furnished hotel. You just show up and sleep there; you can't repaint the walls or change the plumbing. (e.g., Google Workspace, Salesforce). PaaS (Platform as a Service): Renting a serviced apartment. The furniture is there, the utilities are hooked up, and you just bring your clothes and cook. Great for speed, but you have less layout control. (e.g., Heroku, Google App Engine). IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): Renting an empty plot of land or a bare concrete shell. You get the raw foundation—virtual servers (compute), storage, and networking—and you build, wire, and configure everything else.

articles.title: HTTP 200, zero bytes
articles.excerpt: Originally published at tothenoc.substack.com The site was up for twelve days. It was also broken for twelve days. The stylesheet of one of our sites went from 18,496 bytes to zero. The server kept se…
articles.body: Originally published at tothenoc.substack.com The site was up for twelve days. It was also broken for twelve days. The stylesheet of one of our sites went from 18,496 bytes to zero. The server kept serving it. Status 200, every request, for twelve days. Nothing was down. The pages answered, the uptime check was happy, the logs were clean. The site just had no design anymore. How it happened: a small working script, left in the web root since May. Called with no parameters, it used its defaults: write, to that stylesheet, an empty string. It wrote nothing over the file and printed the new length. In the access log the request looks harmless: 200, one byte. That one byte was the digit 0. The worse part came after. I wanted the file back and there was nowhere to take it from.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.
